name: Denominator Numeral Construction

dimensions.form: Cardinal noun with determiner; may take plural morphology
dimensions.meaning: Denotes a token of a numerical type (score, label, symbol)
dimensions.function: Refers to instances of numerals as objects

1.definition: Cardinal noun denotes a token numeral (score, written symbol, etc.)

examples.note: Plural cardinal noun for multiple tokens

constraints.description: Behaves as count noun; takes determiners and plural morphology.
Denotes a token or instance of a numeral, not an abstract number.

projection.target: I rolled three tens describes three tokens of the value ten, rather than a count of ten objects. The lexical noun takes its own plural marking and appears under a separate cardinal determiner.
projection.evidence: The numeral paper distinguishes the count noun for a token or score from arithmetic name and quantificational uses.

curious.title: A ten, three tens
curious.summary: A number word can work like an ordinary noun, naming an instance of a number such as a score.
curious.body: In I rolled a ten, the word ten isn't counting anything. It names a score of ten. It behaves like an ordinary noun: it has a determiner, a, and it can be plural, as in She drew three tens. Three tens means three instances of the value ten, not ten objects. The same works for ratings, as in That's a perfect ten. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Think of a game or contest with scores. How would you name a score of seven as an item, with a before it?

teacher.summary: Helps explain number words used as count nouns, such as a ten and three tens.
teacher.explain: In this use, a cardinal functions as a noun denoting a token or instance of a numeral (a score, a label, a written symbol), not an abstract number. It behaves as a count noun: it takes determiners and plural morphology. I rolled three tens describes three tokens of the value ten, not a count of ten objects. The noun takes its own plural marking and appears under a separate cardinal determinative, as in three tens. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Cardinal here is a noun, not the determinative use of a number as in three dogs.

contrasts.note: Three tokens of the value ten.

watch_for: A learner might read three tens as ten objects counted three times, when it means three tokens of the value ten.
A learner might think a cardinal cannot take a plural ending when it is used as a noun.
teacher.activity: Students play a dice or card game and describe their results with a number noun (I rolled a six, I drew two fives). They then say whether the number counts objects or names a score.

child.hook: Can a number word have a plural, like tens?
child.explain: A number can name a score or a card. I rolled a ten. You can even add an s, as in three tens. That means three of them, each one a ten.
child.play: Roll two dice or draw cards a few times. Describe each result with a number word, like a six. If you get the same number twice, give it an s.

checked.note: Fixed: child.explain no longer says the three tens are rolls (the entry's example is a card draw); curious.body now says 'a score of ten'; cut the unsupported traditional-names sentence in teacher.terms.
